subject: Stan for myriads of parameters in a linear regression model

messages.author: 145936f19be1abc9
messages.subject: Stan for myriads of parameters in a linear regression model
parts:
Hello guys,

I have the following issue:

Problem:
In breeding, it is common to regress observations on the allele count of molecular markers, or simply said, some vector with observations y on a set of predictors that take on values {0,1,2}. Different methods use different priors for the distributions of the effects, but that does not matter. The point is that there is possibly a giant number of predictors, say 50,000. Depending on the priors, either Gibbs-Sampling or Metropolis-within-Gibbs is commonly used to cycle sequentially through all those effects, implemented in some fast language like C++.

Question:
Is it generally possible to fit such a model in a reasonable time using Stan, possibly through some hack or whatever?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Stan for myriads of parameters in a linear regression model
parts:
Have you tried it? 50,000 parameters isn't a problem per se as long as you have enough RAM. We try to avoid hacks, but perhaps you can make things go faster by doing your own sparse multiplication, as in this model block below:

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  vector<lower=0,upper=2>[K] X[N];
  real y[N];
}
parameters {
  vector[K] beta;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  vector[N] mu;
  for(n in 1:N) {
    mu[n] <- 0;
    for(k in 1:K) if(X[n][k] != 0) mu[n] <- mu[n] + X[n][k] * beta[k];
  }
  y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
  // priors
}

Your model is probably not that simple, but that is the basic idea.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Stan for myriads of parameters in a linear regression model
parts:
50K parameters shouldn't be a problem. If they're correlated,
then NUTS is probably going to be faster than Gibbs unless you
can do the whole GLM in a conjugate way with Gibbs.

How many observations?

It might also help to standardize the 0/1/2 inputs if you're
going to use them as a scalar predictor.

If there's a lot of sparseness, it'd be a win to create a dedicated
sparse-data indexing structure. There are examples in the LDA section
of the manual, but it should be pulled out into its own chapter. I
added a new comment to the next manual issue to remind me to do that.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/786#issuecomment-52807162

Also if there's a lot of sparseness or a lot of correlation among
the predictors, you'll need stronger priors on the coefficients.

- Bob

messages.author: 29f6a893ff2525e2
messages.subject: Re: Stan for myriads of parameters in a linear regression model
parts:
I'm a little confused.

Sometimes one tries to create a subset of models with a restricted number of parameters. There are criteria such as AICc etc. etc. etc. The problem is then to find the best subset according to that criteria.

Nowadays, with model averaging, one tries to create a set of models, and you can use MH to choose between the models to create an ensemble. This is a 0-1 problem on each parameter, using MH each time you flip a parameter. You can still use AICc or BIC as your likelihood.  You end up with an equi-probable ensemble of models.

Clearly, for this problem, NUTS is not suitable as there are no derivatives.

But maybe the OP means something completely different? I am probably completely misunderstanding.

If there are 50K predictors, how many data points do you have?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan for myriads of parameters in a linear regression model
parts:
Setting computation costs aside, I prefer not to do model selection or model averaging in this way, instead I prefer to do continuous model expansion.  We discuss this point in chapter 7 of BDA3.  That said, sometimes computation is an issue.

Also, I don’t think BIC makes much sense.  It’s an issue that I discussed in my 1995 paper with Rubin.  I prefer WAIC.
A
